title: The Bias–Variance Tradeoff
hook: Too simple and your model misses the pattern; too flexible and it chases noise. Generalization lives between the two.
key_points: High bias means underfitting — the model is too simple to capture the real relationship.
High variance means overfitting — the model is too sensitive to the particular training sample.
Generalization error reflects both, so reducing one often increases the other.
Model complexity is the dial: increase it and bias falls while variance tends to rise.
content_html: The bias–variance tradeoff is the classic lens for thinking about why models fail to generalize. Bias is error from a model being too simple to represent the truth; variance is error from a model being so flexible that it swings around with each new training sample. The art is balancing the two to minimize total error on unseen data.
extra_html:
How it works

Picture fitting a curve to scattered points. A straight line is high bias: it can't bend to the real shape, so it's wrong in a consistent way. A wildly wiggly curve is high variance: it threads every point but would look completely different on a fresh sample. As you increase model complexity, bias generally drops and variance generally grows, and generalization error traces out a tradeoff between them.

Why it matters

This framing turns vague worries about "underfitting" and "overfitting" into a single dial — model complexity — that you can reason about. It tells you whether to add capacity or add regularization, and it explains why blindly making a model bigger doesn't always help.

related.title: Overfitting & Regularization
related.hook: A model that aces its training data but flops on anything new hasn't learned — it has memorized. Regularization is the cure.

flashcards.prompt: What does high bias indicate about a model?

choices.text: It is too simple to capture the real relationship (underfitting)
It is too sensitive to the particular training sample
It has memorized the training noise

flashcards.explanation_html: High bias is underfitting error — like a straight line that can't bend to the real shape. High variance, by contrast, is overfitting.

flashcards.prompt: What single dial connects bias and variance, and how does it move them?
flashcards.back_html: Model complexity: increasing it generally lowers bias while raising variance, so reducing one error often increases the other.
